title: Maintainer Health Matters More Than GitHub Stars for AI Tool Procurement
author: Dr. Hernani Costa

summary_long:
For open-source AI tool procurement, stars are a leading indicator of attention; maintainer health is a lagging indicator of survival. The article reframes procurement to read ten dimensions separately rather than collapsing them into one number: commit recency, contributor breadth, bus factor, issue response time, release cadence, security responsiveness, license clarity, dependency hygiene, governance model, and enterprise support. For European scale-ups facing EU AI Act sandbox due diligence and DORA third-party-vendor obligations, the same scorecard becomes a compliance artefact, not just a procurement preference.

License clarity is a hard gate at every tier. No LICENSE file means default copyright applies and commercial deployment is unsafe regardless of how popular or technically excellent the project is. Bus factor must be three or higher for enterprise commercial use; the article names three legitimate exceptions and warns against the rest. The exceptions are a paid support contract with an SLA-bound bench (which raises the effective bus factor by the bench size), an escrow agreement granting the right to fork on incapacity, and a tool whose blast radius if abandoned is genuinely contained (a CLI utility used only by the internal engineering team, never embedded in a customer-facing product). Outside those three, single-maintainer is unsafe regardless of how clean the code looks or how responsive the maintainer was last quarter.

Corporate backing alone is not a substitute for contributor breadth. The signal that actually survives a sponsor change is commits from at least three distinct organisations or domains in the last twelve months — what OpenSSF Scorecard's contributor-diversity check measures directly. Read it as "diversity-adjusted bus factor" rather than "is the sponsor on the README." Three Scorecard checks bear on maintainer health: contributor-diversity defends against backed-but-orphaned failure, code-review defends against the no-peer-validation failure, and maintained captures recency plus issue-response cadence as a graded score. A Scorecard below five on contributor-diversity or maintained should block procurement absent a documented mitigation; above seven is the comfortable bar.

A 15-minute rubric distils the ten dimensions into a checklist a platform engineering or security lead can run before any procurement scorecard meeting. The four GitHub REST endpoints (`/repos/{owner}/{repo}/stats/contributors`, `/issues`, `/pulls`, the GitHub Advisory Database cross-check) fit in a 60-line script and need only a token with `public_repo` scope; rate limits handle 30 to 50 candidate repos comfortably per hour.

Three failure patterns recur across the open-source AI corpus. Abandoned-but-popular: a repository whose last commit is more than seven months stale, where security patches do not arrive and dependencies rot. No-license-but-popular: high stars, no LICENSE, default copyright, hard pass. Single-author-bus-factor-one: MIT-licensed code that is safe for personal use and unsafe for production embedding without one of the three named exceptions. The 15-minute rubric catches each pattern in the first five minutes; star counts catch none.

The procurement implication is consistent: twenty minutes of platform engineering or security lead time per candidate tool, against the cost of unwinding a bad procurement six months later when the maintenance gap finally hits production.
